PIPS Group Project

PIPS Group

Introduction

This project was developed for the Programming in Psychological Science course at the University of Amsterdam.

The project investigates psychological data and aims to combine data exploration, statistical analyses, visualisations, and an interactive component.

Dataset

The dataset (Mentalillness.csv, Kaggle) contains 3,753 synthetic participants with 53 binary DSM-5 symptoms and criteria (0 = absent, 1 = present) and 5 binary diagnoses: bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety disorder, and PTSD. It is stored in the data folder.

Because the original column names are long, we first build a variable key that gives each column a short name and records which disorder and DSM-5 criterion it belongs to. The key is saved as data/variable_key.csv. We then load the data with these short names and check that every value is 0 or 1.

source("src/r/functions_data.R")
source("src/r/functions_variable_key.R")

variable_key <- make_variable_key()
save_variable_key(variable_key, "data/variable_key.csv")
## Variable key saved to data/variable_key.csv
clindata <- load_mental_illness("data/Mentalillness.csv", variable_key)
## Check passed: all 58 columns contain only 0 and 1.
knitr::kable(head(variable_key, 10))
original name disorder criterion
Inflated self-esteem bip_inflated_self_esteem bipolar symptom
Distractibility bip_distractibility bipolar symptom
Increase in goal-directed activity bip_goal_directed_activity bipolar symptom
Excessive involvement in activities with high potential for painful consequences bip_risky_activities bipolar symptom
Racing thoughts bip_racing_thoughts bipolar symptom
Decreased need for sleep bip_decreased_sleep_need bipolar symptom
More talkative than usual bip_talkative bipolar symptom
Disorganized thinking or speech scz_disorganized_speech schizophrenia positive
Intrusive memories or flashbacks scz_intrusive_memories schizophrenia other
Diminished emotional expression scz_diminished_expression schizophrenia other

DSM rules

The diagnoses in the dataset follow fixed counting rules. The script test_dsm_rules.R rebuilds all five diagnoses from the symptom columns (with apply_dsm_rules()) and checks them in two ways.

First, it checks that the rebuilt diagnoses match the diagnoses in the data for every participant.

knitr::kable(rule_check)
disorder n_observed n_rebuilt n_match percent_match
bipolar 2909 2909 3753 100
depression 1845 1845 3753 100
anxiety 1622 1622 3753 100
schizophrenia 3167 3167 3753 100
ptsd 203 203 3753 100

Tests

Second, it tests the rules on made-up participants placed exactly at a cutoff (or just below it), whose diagnosis we know in advance. This is where mistakes like > instead of >= would show up.

knitr::kable(test_results)
test passed
Bipolar: 3 symptoms = yes, 2 = no TRUE
Depression: 5 symptoms = yes, 4 = no TRUE
Anxiety: needs 2 symptoms AND duration TRUE
Schizophrenia: positive symptom needed, 2 items in total TRUE
PTSD: all minimums = yes, missing G or 1 D item = no TRUE
Thresholds: bipolar cutoff 2 diagnoses someone with 2 symptoms TRUE

Statistical analysis

The script analyses.R runs the tests and plots.R makes the figures.

Worked example

To show how each test works, we test whether depressed mood is related to a depression diagnosis. A chi-square test compares the observed counts with the counts expected if the two were unrelated; phi gives the size of the relation.

example_table
##    
##        0    1
##   0 1236  686
##   1  672 1159
example_test
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
## 
## data:  example_table
## X-squared = 284.84, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
round(example_phi, 3)
## [1] 0.276

Depressed mood was related to a depression diagnosis, χ²(1) = 284.84, p < .001, φ = .28.

Symptoms and diagnoses

We repeated this test for every symptom against every diagnosis (53 × 5 = 265 tests) and corrected the p-values for multiple testing (FDR).

knitr::kable(association_summary)
symptom_vs_diagnosis n_tests n_significant phi_min phi_max
same disorder 53 37 -0.023 0.895
other disorder 212 0 -0.039 0.045 
heatmap_plot

37 of 53 symptoms were related to their own diagnosis, and none of the 212 symptom–other-diagnosis pairs were related. Each diagnosis depends only on its own symptoms. The 16 non-significant symptoms are all PTSD symptoms: PTSD needs all eight criteria at once, so a single symptom barely changes the odds.

Comorbidity

For every pair of diagnoses, we compared how many participants have both with how many would have both by chance.

knitr::kable(comorbidity, digits = 3)
disorder_1 disorder_2 observed expected ratio chi_square p p_fdr
bipolar schizophrenia 2446 2454.8 1.00 0.80 0.372 0.532
bipolar depression 1427 1430.1 1.00 0.04 0.840 0.840
bipolar anxiety 1273 1257.2 1.01 1.45 0.228 0.457
bipolar ptsd 166 157.3 1.05 1.99 0.159 0.457
schizophrenia depression 1543 1556.9 0.99 1.46 0.227 0.457
schizophrenia anxiety 1358 1368.7 0.99 0.86 0.353 0.532
schizophrenia ptsd 175 171.3 1.02 0.40 0.525 0.609
depression anxiety 807 797.4 1.01 0.36 0.548 0.609
depression ptsd 86 99.8 0.86 3.68 0.055 0.315
anxiety ptsd 101 87.7 1.15 3.46 0.063 0.315 
comorbidity_plot

No pair co-occurred more or less often than expected by chance (all FDR p > .31). Comorbidity in this dataset is pure chance, unlike in real clinical data.

Symptom count and diagnosis

steps_plot

For bipolar and depression, the proportion diagnosed jumps from 0 to 1 exactly at the cutoff. For anxiety it levels off at about .50, because the diagnosis also needs the 6-month duration item, which half of participants have. For schizophrenia it rises gradually, because a positive symptom is also needed. The dip at 6 anxiety symptoms reflects chance in a small group (n = 66).
